claims.text: The catalyst is a nanoscale Pt-based alloy, exemplified by a PtPd-based ternary alloy.
The catalyst is prepared by electrochemical dealloying.
The catalyst has a partially dealloyed structure at the start of operation.
Potential cycling promotes natural surface realloying in the catalyst.
Holding the catalyst at constant potential inhibits realloying relative to potential cycling.
Ethanol oxidation involves a 12-electron and 12-proton process.
Dynamic surface realloying maintains compressive strain exceeding 4%.
Potential cycling continuously renews an active, strained catalyst surface through realloying.
Realloying-induced compressive strain adjusts the adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The adjusted intermediate binding energies lower activation barriers and improve reaction kinetics.
Dynamic realloying and its associated strain enhance catalyst durability.
Cycling conditions that enable realloying will produce higher ethanol-oxidation activity than constant-potential conditions.
Cycling conditions that enable realloying will improve ethanol-oxidation selectivity.
Cycling conditions that enable realloying will improve catalyst durability.
Constant-potential operation will produce lower active strain and diminished catalytic performance.
The proposed mechanism applies under actively cycled fuel-cell potentials but may fail under static or low-potential conditions where realloying is not triggered.

contradictions.description: The experimental arm intended to remain at constant potential is to be evaluated using cyclic voltammetry and long-term testing described as occurring under cycling conditions; those measurements could introduce the potential cycling that the intervention is intended to exclude.
